title: Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?

paper.title: Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose complex tasks and delegate subtasks to different large language model (LLM) agents and tools. Prior studies have reported the superior accuracy performance of MAS across diverse domains, enabled by long-horizon context tracking and error correction through role-specific agents. However, the design and deployment of MAS incur higher complexity and runtime cost compared to single-agent systems (SAS).
Meanwhile, frontier LLMs, such as OpenAI-o3 and Gemini-2.5-Pro, have rapidly advanced in long-context reasoning, memory retention, and tool usage, mitigating many limitations that originally motivated MAS designs. In this paper, we conduct an extensive empirical study comparing MAS and SAS across various popular agentic applications. We find that the benefits of MAS over SAS diminish as LLM capabilities improve, and we propose efficient mechanisms to pinpoint the error-prone agent in MAS. Furthermore, the performance discrepancy between MAS and SAS motivates our design of a hybrid agentic paradigm, request cascading between MAS and SAS, to improve both efficiency and capability. Our design improves accuracy by 1.1-12% while reducing deployment costs by up to 20% across various agentic applications.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In the face of growing complexity and interactivity in LLM-based applications, multi-agent systems (MAS) are gaining traction across a wide range of domains. In MAS architectures, complex tasks are decomposed and delegated to specialized agents—each instantiated as an LLM with a defined role—who coordinate through structured natural language exchanges [ 37 , 4 ] . This paradigm is increasingly adopted in areas such as software engineering, where agent roles like product manager, architect, developer, and tester collaborate to transform high-level requirements into production-quality code [ 19 , 32 ] ; mathematical reasoning, where agents debate and refine proofs [ 13 , 27 ] ; and scientific discovery, including hypothesis generation, peer critique, and experiment design [ 15 , 23 ] . Prior studies have shown the superior accuracy performance of MAS over single-agent systems (SAS) in collaborative reasoning and human-aligned workflows [ 28 ] . By modularizing and distributing responsibilities across agents with dedicated working memory, external tool access, and the ability to critique peer outputs, MAS paradigms support long-horizon context and planning, iterative refinement, and error correction within and across agents. However, the design and deployment of MAS introduce significant complexity. Defining agent roles, capabilities, and coordination logic demands substantial engineering effort upfront, while runtime execution incurs overheads such as increased latency and token costs. Diagnosing failure modes in MAS becomes even more challenging, with recent work showing that MAS can severely degrade due to coordination breakdowns or misaligned agent behaviors [ 3 ] . Meanwhile, frontier LLMs—such as OpenAI-o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro—are rapidly improving in long-context reasoning, memory, and tool usage, challenging many limitations that originally motivated MAS designs. This evolving landscape raises two pressing questions: How does the MAS paradigm compare to the increasingly capable SAS paradigm? Moreover, how can we navigate the tradeoffs between output quality and cost-efficiency for the practical deployment of agentic systems? Figure 1: Overview of the paper. We present a comprehensive empirical comparison of MAS and SAS paradigms, and introduce cost-effective optimizations to improve their efficiency and effectiveness. To this end, as shown in Figure 1 , we first studied the performance of both MAS and SAS paradigms across 15 representative and widely adopted agentic tasks (§ 3 ), spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and travel planning. Our evaluation includes both proprietary models (Gemini-2.0-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Pro, and GPT-4o) and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-4). We notice that (i) MAS are capable of solving complex tasks that SAS fails to handle; (ii) However, as LLMs grow more capable, the performance gap between MAS and SAS narrows on complex tasks, while MAS continues to face significant efficiency challenges; and (iii) In simple tasks, MAS may even underperform SAS due to overthinking. To investigate the root causes underlying these findings, we adopt a first-principles approach and abstract MAS execution as a dependency graph , where nodes represent agents and edges denote inter-agent communications (i.e., responses). We identify three primary sources of MAS defects: • Node-Level Defect : The performance of both MAS and SAS are bottlenecked by a critical agent responsible for the most difficult subtask, capping MAS performance. • Edge-Level Defect : Errors arise when a downstream agent becomes overwhelmed by (overthinking) inputs from upstream agents, compromising its ability to reason effectively. • Path-Level Defect : Indecisive errors can propagate through chains of agent interactions, ultimately leading to incorrect final outputs. However, identifying and mitigating these defects is challenging due to the variety of agentic applications. To address this, we propose a confidence-guided tracing method that considers both the confidence and output quality of agents to pinpoint critical agents —those that bottleneck overall MAS performance, whereby we prioritize augmenting the critical agents for better cost-effectiveness. In light of the performance discrepancy between SAS and MAS, we further introduce agent routing and agent cascade paradigms to selectively offload requests between SAS and MAS, thereby unlocking new accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs in agentic system deployments. Our evaluations show that our hybrid paradigm improves accuracy by 1.1-12% while reducing costs by up to 88.1%. Overall, we make the following contributions: • We conduct an extensive study of MAS and SAS deployments across 15 representative datasets over 7 tasks using 9 frameworks. • We propose a novel attribution method to categorize and diagnose MAS defects by identifying critical agents that bottleneck overall performance. • We introduce agent routing and cascade paradigms to integrate SAS and MAS, unlocking improved accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Multi-agent Applications.
sections.text: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are gaining traction in various domain-specific tasks, typically featuring specialized agents with role-specific prompts and behaviors. For instance, MetaGPT [ 19 ] introduces a meta-programming framework that formalizes human workflows into structured multi-agent collaborations to improve code generation quality. ChatDev [ 32 ] employs agents with distinct business roles (CEO, CTO, programmer, reviewer, tester), using structured chat chains to guide their interactions and employing communicative dehallucination to reduce coding errors. In scientific reasoning, [ 13 ] shows that collaborative agent debates can improve factual consistency. Other systems have demonstrated the utility of MAS in solving complex tasks across domains including mathematical reasoning [ 27 ] , scientific discovery [ 15 , 23 ] , healthcare [ 7 ] , travel planning [ 37 ] , game development [ 4 , 41 ] , and financial trading [ 40 ] .

sections.heading: Optimizing Agentic Systems.
sections.text: Despite its promising performance, MAS often involves large design complexity and operational overhead. To support long-horizon context tracking, Agent Workflow Memory [ 38 ] introduces a memory module tailored for web navigation tasks. Similarly, StateFlow [ 39 ] improves task-solving performance by controlling and reasoning over internal agent states during execution. To automate the optimization of generative AI workflows, Cognify [ 16 ] proposes a hierarchical search strategy that adaptively tunes parameters to enhance output quality and efficiency. Ayo [ 34 ] optimizes end-to-end MAS performance by modeling agent workflows as primitive-level dataflow graphs for efficient resource scheduling. To diagnose failure modes in agentic workflows, [ 26 ] shows that embedding structured error-type relationships into chain-of-thought (CoT) and tree-of-thought (ToT) prompts can improve error classification in logic programming. Other studies [ 43 , 3 ] explore the use of LLMs as judges to identify failure points and trace error attribution.

sections.heading: 3 Multi-agent or Single-agent Systems?
sections.text: With the skyrocketing interest in MAS and the rapid advancement of LLM capabilities, it is pressing to reassess agentic system designs. We begin by formalizing the quality and efficiency requirements of agentic applications (§ 3.1 ). Next, we present a comprehensive performance study comparing MAS and SAS across a range of tasks (§ 3.2 ), followed by an analysis of the MAS defects (§ 3.3 ).

sections.text: Practical agentic systems aim for high accuracy while also maintaining low deployment cost (e.g., monetary cost for API calls). Going beyond the diminishing accuracy benefits, we observe that MAS incurs substantially higher costs due to complex interactions among agents. Table 3 shows that across seven datasets, MAS consumes 4–220 × \times more input (prefill) tokens than its SAS counterpart. Even assuming perfect context reuse where we directly reuse upstream outputs as downstream inputs without repeating the prefill phase, MAS still requires 2–12 × \times more tokens for response generation (decoding). Such cross-agent interaction has been reported to significantly improve accuracy. However, we observe that MAS loses this advantage as LLM capabilities advance. Together with its substantial efficiency gap, this calls for a reassessment of whether MAS remains the off-the-shelf solution for agentic system deployment.

sections.heading: 3.3 Why MAS Is Losing Its Edge?
sections.text: We next investigate why the performance gains of MAS diminish, and in some cases, even fall behind SAS. To this end, we conduct a datapoint-level analysis: for each example in the dataset, we compare the correctness of the outputs from MAS and SAS paradigms. Specifically, Both Pass indicates that both MAS and SAS produce correct answers; Both Fail means both are incorrect; MAS Win denotes that MAS is correct while SAS is not; SAS Win follows similar logic. Figure 2: SAS can achieve comparable accuracy performance to MAS. As shown in Figure 2 , we summarize three observations: • Observation 1: Across all datasets, the majority of examples fall into the ”ties” category ( Both Pass and Both Fail ), accounting for approximately 80% of the total; • Observation 2: There are non-negligible cases of SAS Wins while MAS fails; • Observation 3: As we switch to a stronger model (e.g., from Gemini-1.5-Flash to Gemini-2.0-Flash ), the number of Both Pass increases while SAS Wins and MAS Wins remain relatively unchanged. These trends hold consistently across both the OpenAI and Gemini models. Leveraging our graph-based formulation of agentic execution (§ 3.1 ), we next summarize the underlying factors leading to MAS underperformance. Node-Level Defect: The performance of both MAS and SAS is bottlenecked by the capability of the critical agent responsible for solving the most challenging subtask. Our conclusion stems from Observation 1 , where the majority of cases fall under Both Pass or Both Fail , suggesting that task decomposition in MAS often has limited impact: if the task is simple, SAS can solve it; if it is too difficult, MAS still fails. Observation 3 reinforces our conclusion, as the increase in Both Pass cases with stronger base models does not correspond to a notable rise in MAS Wins . This indicates that stronger models benefit both systems similarly, and MAS fails to yield a higher win rate than SAS under more capable LLMs. There are exceptions like AIME, which is considered the most difficult math dataset. As such, MAS is able to consistently outperform SAS on this dataset, illustrating its ability to solve extremely difficult tasks. Edge-Level Defect: The downstream agent gets overwhelmed by inputs from other agents. In MAS, agents often engage in multi-way conversations or prolonged iterative refinements. It is common for certain nodes in the MAS execution graph to exhibit high in-degree, such as the summarizer in math debates or the response synthesizer in RAG-based documentation systems [ 25 , 13 ] . However, the influx of information from upstream agents can overwhelm the receiving agent, leading to overthinking on edge cases and ultimately producing incorrect results. We hypothesize that this contributes to Observation 2 , where SAS consistently outperforms MAS on a non-trivial subset of examples. To validate our hypothesis, we conducted an extensive case study manually. For instance, in the code generation task using the SelfCol. [ 6 ] framework, the problem analyst and tester agents introduce too many unnecessary corner cases. This overloads the coder agent, leading to task failure. We provide more examples in the appendix. ⬇ [Analyzer] You should implement the file name checker step by step ... [Coder] Sure , here is the code : .... [Reviewer] Consider edge_cases : [" Empty string ", " String with only spaces ", " String ending with a space ", " String with multiple spaces between words "...] [Coder] Updated code : ... Such a phenomenon is analogous to the overthinking of the reasoning model [ 8 ] , but rather than being "lost" in thinking, the agent becomes overwhelmed by inputs from upstream agents. Though we might mitigate this defect by better prompt engineering or extended context lengths, the root cause lies in hallucination [ 33 ] and overthinking, which are intrinsic challenges of LLMs themselves. MAS aggravates the problem as agents process much more data. Path-Level Defect: Indecisive errors propagate along the path and become fatal. As information flows between agents, crucial context can be lost or diluted [ 44 ] , especially when intermediate outputs are summarized or filtered before being passed along (e.g., from multi-hops ago). Even a small piece of lost information can cause irreversible errors in downstream reasoning due to a snowball effect. In contrast, SAS has full access to its history, though still limited by context length. Emerging models with extended long-context capabilities [ 10 , 29 ] help alleviate this issue. We hypothesize that this defect contributes to Observation 2 , where SAS consistently outperforms MAS in a portion of cases, and conducted an extensive case study to validate it. We provide an example from the math reasoning task below, which shows that a correct solution proposed in an earlier round was lost during summarization before being passed to the next agent. This loss is unrecoverable, as downstream agents no longer have access to the full previous results. ⬇ [Round X-1, Solver B] The number of sets in Bob ’ s list is given by $ \ sum_ { a \ in A } 2^{ a -1} = 2024 $ ... So the answer is {{55}} [Summarizer] : Results from three solvers are inconsistent ... [Round X, Solver B] The error lies in the misinterpretation of the problem statement . The number 2024 represents the total number of sets B , not the size of set A ... So the answer is {{28}} Unlike decisive errors studied in previous literature [ 43 ] , these propagation-induced errors are difficult to detect and backtrace, as it requires global knowledge to determine which information can be safely diluted and which must be retained. However, the design principle of MAS—the division of tasks—runs counter to this requirement.

sections.heading: Summary:
sections.text: Think twice before adopting MAS deployment. While MAS still offers advantages such as better privacy [ 45 ] , improved parallelism, and democratization [ 35 ] , our extensive real-world evaluations reveal that MAS is not a one-size-fits-all solution for diverse tasks. In fact, it often suffers from cost-ineffectiveness. Consequently, naively converting a SAS solution into an MAS one may yield less accuracy improvement than expected, while incurring substantially higher costs.

sections.heading: 4 Towards Cost-Effective Agentic Deployments
sections.text: The intricate accuracy-cost tradeoff in MAS and SAS has led to substantial deployment challenges. We next explore the design space for automatically improving agentic systems. Specifically, we (i) identify and augment the critical execution path in MAS to enhance accuracy (§ 4.1 ), and (ii) introduce a hybrid SAS-MAS deployment paradigm for better accuracy and cost efficiency (§ 4.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Augmenting MAS Critical Path.
sections.text: Our studies (§ 3.3 ) reveal that MAS can suffer from node-, edge-, and path-level defects that limit accuracy. However, identifying these defects is challenging due to the diversity of tasks and the intricate interactions among agents. Verifying every intermediate message introduces exponential complexity and overhead as workflow depth increases. Moreover, most existing MAS frameworks invoke LLM agents through public APIs (e.g., OpenAI or Gemini) [ 20 , 31 , 13 ] , which offer limited control over internal mechanisms such as KV cache management or fine-tuning, further constraining optimization opportunities. A strawman solution is to use the most advanced model for every agent, but this incurs excessive cost, as these models are significantly more expensive to run. As discussed in Section 3.3 , one promising strategy is to selectively upgrade critical agents rather than uniformly upgrading all agents. However, this is nontrivial, as it requires systematically identifying error-prone nodes and edges in the execution graph—a challenge that remains open-ended. To address this, we propose a lightweight, automated probing mechanism to detect critical agents. Figure 3: We propose a lightweight, confidence-guided probing method to identify critical agents for improvement (left), and further improve cost-effectiveness by integrating SAS and MAS paradigms.

sections.heading: Confidence-Guided Critical Path Tracing.
sections.text: Our key insight is to assign differentiated rewards to agents based on both their confidence and the quality of the final output. This enables us to prioritize the augmentation of agents that bottleneck successful outcomes. Consider the MATH-DEBATE framework [ 13 ] , where agents propose solutions and a majority vote determines the final answer. If the final output is correct (or incorrect), each agent contributing to it receives a reward (or penalty). However, this naive scheme treats all contributing agents equally, failing to account for their differing contribution levels. To address this, we incorporate confidence scores into the reward function. Each agent is prompted to self-report its confidence level on a scale from 1 (least confident) to 10 (most confident), formatted as “Agent Response [Confidence Level]” . Understandably, an agent that is both confident and correct should be rewarded more than one that is unsure or incorrect. As shown in Figure 3 , after completing a request r ∈ R r\in R , we propagate the quality of its final output Q r Q_{r} , which is defined by a task-specific evaluation metric (e.g., Q r = 1 Q_{r}=1 if the output is correct, and 0 otherwise). Together with the response confidence c i c_{i} of agent i i , its reward score, I i I_{i} , is updated as: I i = ∑ r ∈ R Q r ⋅ c i + ( 1 − c i ) ​ ( 1 − Q r ) , where ​ Q r = { 1 if final output correct 0 if final output wrong I_{i}=\sum_{r\in R}Q_{r}\cdot c_{i}+(1-c_{i})(1-Q_{r}),\quad\text{where }Q_{r}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if final output correct}\\ 0&\text{if final output wrong}\end{cases} Our confidence-based critical path tracing identifies the agent that presents the greatest reward bottleneck. To show the effectiveness of our design, we use node augmentation to boost the MAS performance in a cost-efficient way. Specifically, we identify the agent with the lowest reward score and upgrade its model to a more capable version (e.g., replacing Gemini-1.5-Flash with Gemini-2.0-Flash ). This targeted enhancement reduces the likelihood of localized errors and strengthens the agent’s ability to solve previously unresolvable subtasks. We use a math reasoning task (AIME) to demonstrate the effectiveness of our design. Here we assign three agents (solvers) with different model series, Llama series (Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b) for agent A, GPT series (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) for agent B, and Gemini series (Gemini-1.5-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Flash) for agent C. We performed two experiment setup: (i) Agent Upgrading , where the original agent pipeline consists of (Llama3.1-8b, GPT-3.5, Gemini-1.5-Flash) and we hope to identify which agent to upgrade to its premium model to maximize accuracy performance; and (ii) Agent Downgrading , where the original agent pipeline consists of (Llama3.1-70b, GPT-4, Gemini-2.0-Flash) and we hope to identify which agent to downgrade to its basic model to minimize accuracy drop. Figure 4(a) shows the accuracy difference after flipping each model, and it reports that our guided tracing approach identifies the most important agent to flip when the budget only allows one. Our decision is optimal for both cases, bringing the most (least) performance gain (drop). (a) Aug. sections.heading: 4.2 Integrating SAS-MAS Paradigms.
sections.text: Augmenting the critical path makes MAS more suitable for complex problems that benefit from specialized roles. However, this still comes at deployment cost. In contrast, SAS tends to be more efficient and effective for simpler, well-scoped tasks. More subtly, investing more resources in MAS does not necessarily yield better performance than SAS (§ 3.2 ). As such, one would expect a hybrid paradigm that strategically combines MAS and SAS to leverage their respective design sweet spots. However, integrating MAS and SAS paradigms is non-trivial due to the wide variability in task complexity and application domains. Moreover, a practical solution must be request-dependent and cost-efficient. To this end, we introduce two primary strategies: Agent Routing and Agent Cascade for different scenarios.

sections.heading: Agent Routing.
sections.text: The key idea behind agent routing is to use an LLM-based rater to assess the complexity of each request and decide whether to route it to an SAS or MAS system. This strategy is broadly applicable across diverse workloads. Here, the rater assigns a difficulty score to each incoming request. Based on a user-defined threshold, requests with scores above the threshold are routed to MAS, while those below are handled by SAS. The routing design offers users flexibility to balance accuracy and cost. Suppose a proportion p p of requests are routed to MAS, and the remaining ( 1 − p 1-p ) to SAS. Then, the total cost of agent routing can be defined as: C Rater ​ ( r ) + p ⋅ C MAS ​ ( r ) + ( 1 − p ) ⋅ C SAS ​ ( r ) , C_{\text{Rater}}(r)+p\cdot C_{\text{MAS}}(r)+(1-p)\cdot C_{\text{SAS}}(r), where C ⁡ ( r ) C(r) denotes the cost of processing request r r . The rater adds only minimal overhead because it relies on a system prompt that can be effectively cached and produces only a small, constant number of tokens representing the difficulty score. The accuracy of this routing approach depends on the rater’s capability and the choice of the threshold value. Figure 4(b) shows the results on the math reasoning task (GSM8K + AIME dataset) with Gemini-2.0-Flash as the rater, achieving 2% better accuracy at 50% cost compared with MAS baseline. Note that we did not fine-tune a difficulty rating model to demonstrate the generalizability of our solution, so the reported performance can be viewed as a lower bound. Nonetheless, we observe that agent routing generally achieves higher accuracy than SAS and, with a properly selected threshold value (routing easy requests to SAS and hard requests to MAS), it can even outperform MAS (§ 3.3 ). Figure 4(c) also shows that the overhead introduced by the LLM rater is negligible.

In many tasks (e.g., exact math problems and code generation), the final output of agentic systems can be efficiently verified. This enables an agent cascade design that first routes the request to SAS to obtain an initial output. The output is then evaluated for its quality (e.g., correctness). If the result from SAS is satisfactory, it is returned directly; otherwise, the request is escalated to MAS. Suppose a proportion p p of requests are passed through SAS, while the remaining ( 1 − p 1-p ) requests have to be escalated to MAS, the cost of agent cascade can be defined as: ( 1 − p ) ⋅ C MAS ​ ( r ) + C SAS ​ ( r ) (1-p)\cdot C_{\text{MAS}}(r)+C_{\text{SAS}}(r) As shown in the formula, this cascade paradigm is justified as long as the cost of SAS is significantly lower than that of MAS, which has been confirmed in Table 3 . This makes the overhead of a failed SAS attempt negligible. Conversely, a successful SAS attempt—the “short path”—yields substantial savings by avoiding the costly MAS. We evaluate our cascade paradigm across a diverse set of agentic applications. As shown in Table 4 , agent cascade achieves consistent accuracy improvement, up to 12% over MAS and SAS, while lowering cost by 20%.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We present a comprehensive study comparing MAS and SAS across 15 tasks, finding that while MAS excels on complex tasks, SAS is often more efficient and equally effective on simpler ones. We attribute MAS underperformance to node-, edge-, and path-level defects, and introduce a confidence-guided tracing method to identify critical agents. To optimize cost-effectiveness, we propose a hybrid agentic paradigm that selectively offloads requests between MAS and SAS, achieving up to 12% better accuracy and 88.1% cost savings. Our findings offer actionable insights for deploying adaptive, cost-efficient agentic systems. Limitation : Although in this paper, we did extensive analysis across tasks, frameworks, and models, our experiments are mostly focused on agentic systems built upon general-purpose models, rather than fine-tuned models. In addition, this paper focuses on agentic systems for task solving, despite they are the most popular ones. We left those unexplored areas as future work. Broader Impact : This paper challenges the prevailing assumption that MAS outperforms SAS in terms of accuracy. We identify that this misconception arises from fundamental limitations inherent to agentic frameworks. We further advocate for future research in multi-agent systems to place greater emphasis on deployment efficiency rather than accuracy alone.

sections.heading: Appendix A Overview
sections.text: Section B details our experimental setup, tasks, and datasets for reproducibility. Section C presents our full evaluation result. Section D provides ablation studies, including the study of the impact of agent count, reflection rounds, and early stopping. Section E includes case studies illustrating our MAS defect categorization. Finally, Section F lists the prompts used for each task.

sections.heading: Tasks.
sections.text: We conducted experiments on a broad suite of representative tasks: • Code Generation : We focus on tasks that involve generating a single function, code segment, or file. Our evaluation includes datasets such as HumanEval, MBPP, DS-1000, and BigCodeBench, as well as agentic frameworks like SelfCol and MetaGPT. • Software Engineering : These tasks involve integrating multiple functionalities and managing multi-file codebases. We evaluate on SWE-Bench and MAST datasets, using frameworks such as ChatDev, MetaGPT, and HyperAgent. • Math Reasoning : This category includes tasks that require step-by-step problem solving, serving as a standard benchmark for evaluating reasoning capabilities. We include MATH-500, AIME, and GSM8K datasets, and use the MATH-DEBATE framework. • Travel Planning : A common real-world planning scenario, which provides a rich sandbox environment, various tools for accessing nearly four million data records. We use the ItineraryBench dataset and the TDAG framework in the original paper. • Financial Analysis : The task includes sentiment analysis, financial report analysis, and investment suggestion. We use the FinRobot framework with 3 datasets. • RAG-based Question Answering : The task is about question answering with possible external information from retrieve-augmented-generation(RAG). We use the MAS workflow in Cognify [ 17 ] and Ayo [ 35 ] and one dataset. • Scientific Experiment : This tasks is about finding possible improvements from a science journal with LLM. We use the dataset and framework from the original paper.

sections.heading: Frameworks.
sections.text: We follow the popular settings of the aforementioned tasks and run them using the following frameworks: • SelfCol [ 12 ] is a framework comprising an analyzer, a coder, and a tester, originally designed for code generation tasks. We adopt this framework in our experiments but make two key modifications. First, due to the inability to reproduce the original results, which claim that a multi-agent setup improves code generation, we revise the prompts to better align with our tasks. Second, we simplify the architecture from a three-agent to a two-agent system, as the tester does not contribute meaningfully to generation accuracy. • Debate [ 14 ] is a multi-agent reasoning framework involving several solvers and a summarizer. In each round, solvers independently generate solutions, and the summarizer aggregates and returns the summary to the solvers for the next round. We apply this framework to math reasoning tasks, keeping the original prompts unchanged to faithfully replicate and verify results from the original paper. Our default configuration uses 3 agents and 2 debate rounds for win-rate evaluations. • MetaGPT [ 20 ] is a framework that consists of a project manager, an architect, a project manager, an engineer, and a QA engineer. The workflow and message passing are a chain without a loop. We use this framework for both code generation and software engineering tasks. • ChatDev [ 31 ] is a framework that consists of a CEO, a CTO, a programmer, a reviewer, and a tester. The messages are passing along the chain, but there will be multi-round conversations between agents. We tested it on 30 software engineering tasks. • TDAG [ 36 ] is a framework that dynamically decomposes the task into subtasks and generates multiple agents for corresponding subtasks. It includes a main agent to decompose the task, and a generator agent that generates new agents based on the task. We use the framework for the travel planning task. • HyperAgent [ 30 ] is also a framework designed for software engineering. It includes a planner, a navigator, an editor, and an executor. They have a tree-like structure that spans from the planner. • Curie [ 23 ] is a framework that consists of an architect and multiple technicians, with different technicians responsible for different specific subtasks, and the architect plans out the whole procedure. • FinRobot [ 42 ] is the multi-agent workflow used in Cognify [ 17 ] . It includes a group leader and an agent pool, where the leader talks with specialists in the agent pool for possibly multiple rounds until the problem is solved. We use this framework in a financial analysis task. • DocRetrieval is the multi-agent workflow used in cognify [ 17 ] and ayo [ 35 ] . It consists of a retriever and a summarizer, and a query generator, where at each RAG hop, the retriever searches for a document, has it summarized then uses it to generate the query for the next hop, until the answer is found. We use this framework for the RAG-based QA task.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We next provide details of the dataset used in each task and framework. • HumanEval [ 5 ] : A benchmark created by OpenAI consisting of 164 Python programming problems. We use pass@1 as the accuracy metric. • MBPP [ 2 ] : The Mostly Basic Python Problems dataset consists of 1266 crowd-sourced Python programming problems. Each problem includes a task description, code solution, and 3 automated test cases. We use pass@1 as the accuracy metric. • DS-1000 [ 24 ] : A code generation benchmark with 1,000 data science problems spanning seven Python libraries, such as NumPy and Pandas. We use pass@1 as the accuracy metric. • BigCodeBench [ 46 ] (Full and Hard): A benchmark evaluating LLMs with practical and challenging programming tasks. It consists of 1140 problems and 148 hard problems. We use pass@1 as the accuracy metric. • SWE-bench [ 22 ] : A dataset that tests systems’ ability to solve GitHub issues. It collects 2,294 Issue-Pull Request pairs from 12 popular Python repositories. We use % Resolved as an evaluation metric. A problem is considered resolved as long as it passes all unit tests. • MAST [ 3 ] : Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy proposes a programdev dataset that consists of 30 programming tasks. We evaluating this dataset, we use the trace provided in the MAST repository. We use human annotation as the evaluation metric. • AIME (2024 & 2025) [ 1 ] : The American Invitational Mathematics Examination dataset consisting of 30 mathematical problems each year (60 in total). We use exact match on the answer as the accuracy metric. • GSM8K [ 9 ] : A dataset of 8,500 grade school math word problems. We use exact math on the answer as the accuracy metric. • MATH-500 [ 18 ] : A dataset consisting of 500 math problems covering topics like algebra, calculus, and geometry. It is also annotated with a difficulty level. We use exact math on the answer as the accuracy metric. • Hover [ 21 ] : A dataset for multi-hop fact extraction, consisting of 4000 testcases in the validation split. We use exact math and F1 score as the accuracy metric. • FinRobot-Headline [ 42 ] : A dataset of 675 financial microblog messages and 438 news headlines annotated for aspect-based sentiment. Evaluation metrics include F1-score and accuracy. • FinRobot-Financial QA (FiQA) [ 42 ] : A collection of question–answer pairs for opinion-based financial QA, introduced in the FiQA 2018 challenge. We use LLM as the autorater following the original paper. • FinRobot-Sentiment Analysis [ 42 ] : A dataset of financial microblog messages and 438 news headlines annotated for aspect-based sentiment. Evaluation metrics include F1-score and classification accuracy. We randomly choose 300 examples from 3 FinRobot datasets to generally reflect the effectiveness of the FinRobot framework. • TravelPlanner (ItineraryBench) [ 37 ] : A benchmark for travel-planning agents, comprising 1,225 itinerary queries across varied durations and constraints. The evaluation metric is the plan success rate (percentage of constraints satisfied). • Curie [ 23 ] : Paper opensourced an experiment benchmark consisting of 46 tasks across 4 domains within computer science, with different difficulties. The evaluation metrics cover different aspects in design, setup, relationship, and goal, and the final accuracy is the weighted average of those four.

sections.heading: LLM Models.
sections.text: We evaluate a range of frontier LLMs from different model families, including Gemini-2.0-Flash-001, Gemini-2.5-Pro-Preview-0506, GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125, GPT-4o-2024-08-06, LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. We use the default settings of these models for fair comparison. We also include the performance analysis across different temperature settings in Appendix C , reporting consistent findings.

sections.heading: B.2 Confidence Based Tracing
sections.text: We request the agent to output the confidence by concatenating the following prompt to the original prompt: ⬇ Also , provide your confidence in your answer on a scale from 1 ( least confident ) to 10 ( most confident ), in the form : Confidence : X . We will extract the confidence score using regular expressions. The confidence score is recorded for each round. When neither agent reaches an agreement during the majority voting, we will choose the agent with the highest confidence score. Though we hope the confidence to be normalized from 0 to 1, it would be extremely hard for LLM to output an accurate estimation of a float confidence. Therefore, we instead request the model to output the confidence on a scale from 0 to 10 as shown above. Suppose the confidence ranges from 0 to s s , we reformulate the importance score calculation as shown in Section 4.1 as below: I i = ∑ r ∈ R Q r ⋅ c i + ( s − c i ) ​ ( 1 − Q r ) , where ​ Q r = { 1 if final output correct 0 if final output wrong I_{i}=\sum_{r\in R}Q_{r}\cdot c_{i}+(s-c_{i})(1-Q_{r}),\quad\text{where }Q_{r}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if final output correct}\\ 0&\text{if final output wrong}\end{cases} We accumulate the importance score over multiple rounds. For round t t , we update the importance score calculation as below: I i t = I i t − 1 + ∑ r ∈ R Q r ⋅ c i + ( s − c i ) ​ ( 1 − Q r ) , where ​ Q r = { 1 if final output correct 0 if final output wrong I_{i}^{t}=I_{i}^{t-1}+\sum_{r\in R}Q_{r}\cdot c_{i}+(s-c_{i})(1-Q_{r}),\quad\text{where }Q_{r}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if final output correct}\\ 0&\text{if final output wrong}\end{cases}

sections.heading: B.3 Agent Routing
sections.text: We detail our setup for agent routing. Here, we run the Math Debate framework for the Math Reasoning task. Here, we use a synthesized dataset to diversify the spectrum of difficulty by combining AIME and GSM8K. We use the exact match as accuracy, and calculate the number of tokens as prefill_token + 2 * decode_token , following the API price in both Open AI and Gemini, where the output token is twice as expensive as the input token. We use the same parameter setup in the main experiment. We use Gemini-2.0-Flash as a rater with the following generation configuration: temperature=0.3, max_tokens=300 , and leave the prompts for LLM rater in F.4 .

sections.heading: Binary Method.
sections.text: It should be noted that asking the user to define the threshold incurs extra overhead. We also have conducted an experiment by asking the rater to give out a binary classification (i.e., to use SAS or MAS). We give up the distribution of ratings in terms of binary classification here: • AIME: SAS: 0 in total; MAS: 60 in total, [rating, # problem]: [6, 4] [7, 16] [8, 29] [9, 11] • GSM8K: SAS: 1266 in total, [rating, # problem]: [1, 364] [2, 30] [3, 810] [4, 61], [5, 1]; MAS: 53 in total, [rating, # problem]: [3, 7], [4, 29], [5, 8], [6, 9] From the result, we can see that the two methods align pretty well, with only 37 out of 1319 categorized differently.

sections.text: Since we are using LLM-as-a-Judge, it is crucial for us to show that the result is consistent across different models. This further confirms the effectiveness of our method.

sections.heading: B.4 Agent Cascade
sections.text: In the agent cascade design, we use the same generation configuration as in the main experiment. We use 2 * Decode_Token + Prefill_Token to calculate the token cost. It should be noted that the agent cascade uniformly has higher accuracy than SAS and MAS, because as long as either SAS or MAS is correct, it would be correct in the agent cascade. Moreover, note that agent cascade works only if the result can be easily and accurately evaluated, like here we are using exact match and pass@1 . If we have to attribute to a more advanced evaluation method, like human or LLM-as-a-Judge, then the cost of agent cascade would add an extra term for that.

sections.text: To further understand the behavior of the SAS and MAS, we follow the previous research [ 3 ] and analyze 30 human-annotated Software Engineering problems. We use the rubric in the MAST paper and classify the generated program as Pass or Fail . We use Gemini-2.5-Pro for SAS, and use the trace provided in the MAST repository as MAS, which includes two frameworks: MetaGPT and ChatDev. Table 13 and Table 14 show the result. In general, the SAS solved 24 out of 30 problems, outperforming the MAS in ten cases while losing in only one case. We attribute that to the strong capability of the reasoning model of Gemini-2.5-Pro , which further confirms our hypothesis of Node Defect . sections.heading: Impact of Number of Agents.
sections.text: We next study whether the system’s performance grows as we increase the number of agents in it. We use the Debate framework in the Math Reasoning task, and change the number of solves during the debate. Figure 8 shows that most of the time, when we increase the number of solves, the accuracy does not increase. Actually, we notice that even if we only use one agent, the result is still comparable to using more agents. This finding only confirms our Node Defect hypothesis that the whole performance is bounded by the critical agents—weak agents cannot solve the math problem are essentially guessing, and it does not help when we just increase the number of random guesses. We also conduct the experiment of the effect of Summarize (i.e., pass the summary of the previous round to the next round) or just Concatenate (i.e., just dump everything from the previous round to the next round). From Figure 8 , we observe that there is not much difference for the Gemini-2.0-Flash model, while Summarize is worse than Concatenate when using weak models. This also confirms our hypothesis on Path Defect , where the weak summarizer will inevitably lose critical information from the previous round, leading to an accuracy drop.

sections.heading: Impact of Number of Reflection Rounds.
sections.text: We further investigate whether self-reflection helps improve MAS performance. We use the Debate framework for the Math Reasoning task. Figure 9 shows that increasing the number of rounds of debate (reflection) increases accuracy in AIME, but decreases accuracy in GSM8K. This further confirms our Edge Defect hypothesis, where too much redundant information on easy tasks actually makes agents confused and obsessed with corner cases, thus losing accuracy, while reflection on complicated problems is effective.

sections.heading: Impact of Early Stopping.
sections.text: To further confirm our hypothesis of the Edge Defect , we employ a naive “cut off” experiment: In the code generation task with the SelfCol framework, suppose that the agent analyst needs to send to the agent coder its plan that guides it future generation Msg , we choose a cutoff percentage x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] x\in[0,1] , and we only send Msg[:len(Msg) * x] to the agent coder. Here, x = 0 x=0 means no coder has to write the code on their own, and x = 1 x=1 is the original MAS setup. Figure 10 shows that only around 25% of messages actually help in the final accuracy. And for advanced models like Gemini-1.5-Pro or Gemini-2.0-Flash , the coder agent can do pretty well on its own. This further confirms our hypothesis that the system accuracy is bound by the critical agent (code here), and receiving too much information from upstream does not really help.

sections.heading: Impact of Temperature.
sections.text: We further show that our observations remain consistent across different temperature settings (Figure 8 -Figure 10 ). We vary the temperature setting ( T T ) in LLM generation, such as T T = 0, 0.4, and 0.8, and notice consistency across a wide range of tasks, datasets, and models.

sections.heading: Example 2.
sections.text: This is an example from the Code Generation task, using SelfCol as the framework. and Gemini-2.0-Flash as the base model. This is problem 142 from the HumanEval dataset. Problem 142 asks sum squares to treat elements at indices divisible by 3 as squares, and those at indices divisible by 4 (but not 3) as cubes, summing the results. The prompt uses mathematically precise zero-based indexing, but its phrasing—“if its index is a multiple of 3, 4”—is easy to misread. The coder agent interprets this in a human-friendly, one-based way: it adds 1 to each index before applying modulus checks. As a result, index 0 is skipped entirely, and index 3 is wrongly treated as a multiple of 4, causing all hidden tests to fail except the empty list. ⬇ { " task_type ": " function_implementation ", " entry_point ": " sum_squares ", " inputs ": [ { " name ": " lst ", " data_type ": " list [ int ]" } ], " outputs ": { " data_type ": " int " }, " requirements ": [ " Square the integer entry if its index is a multiple of 3.", " Cube the integer entry if its index is a multiple of 4 and not a multiple of 3.", " Do not change the entries in the list whose indexes are not a multiple of 3 or 4.", " Return the sum of all entries ." ], " examples ": [ { " input ": "[1,2,3]", " output ": 6 }, { " input ": "[]", " output ": 0 }, { " input ": "[-1,-5,2,-1,-5]", " output ": -126 } ], " edge_cases ": [ " Empty list ", " List with only one element ", " List with positive and negative numbers ", " List with zero values ", " List where some indices are multiples of both 3 and 4 ( i . e ., multiples of 12)" ], " validation_needs ": [ " Input must be a list .", " List elements must be integers ." ] } Coder Output : def sum_squares ( lst ): """ This function will take a list of integers and square the integer entry if its index is a multiple of 3 and will cube the integer entry if its index is a multiple of 4 and not a multiple of 3. It will not change the entries in the list whose indexes are not multiples of 3 or 4. Examples : For lst = [1,2,3] the output should be 6 For lst = [] the output should be 0 For lst = [-1,-5,2,-1,-5] the output should be -126 """ total = 0 for i , num in enumerate ( lst ): if ( i + 1) % 3 == 0: total += num **2 elif ( i + 1) % 4 == 0: total += num **3 else : total += num return total

sections.text: ⬇ You are an expert in finding all relevant information insider a code repository to answer the query from a planner agent . When you write Python code for action , put the code in a markdown code block with the language set to Python . Write code incrementally and leverage the statefulness of the kernel to avoid repeating code . Always output one action at a time , and wait for the user to execute the code before providing the next action . Only focus on the planner ’ s query . If your first attempts do not provide enough information to resolve the query , try different tools or use tool with different parameters to get the information you need . Think carefully before making a decision . Your tools can provide valuable insights to help you resolve the query . Once you have collected relevant information , you can provide a response to the query with Final Answer , put any code snippet into that summary . Do not repeat your actions ( IMPORTANT !) ### Guidelines : 1. Understanding the query , think step - by - step carefully before decision to propose actions to collect necessary information to resolve the query . 2. Do not repeat your actions . Only generate 1 block of code at one time . 3. Try to use the tools to get the information you need . DO NOT GUESS or refuse to response the planner ’ s request . Planner request is always correct . You may only see part of the information , but the planner sees the whole picture . 4. If one tool does not find the information you need , try another tool . If you open a file , but do not find the information you need , reopen with different start_line and end_line or keywords . 5. Your final answer should only include code snippets that are relevant to query only . ### Important Notes : 1 Only use the provided and predefined functions as the functions . Do not use any other functions . 2. ( single word only , not a combination like sympy . latex ), in this case , _print . 8. open_file : Use this tool to open a file in the codebase , this is useful to read the partial content of the file (40 lines ). sections.text: ⬇ You are a lab technician . Given an input containing an experimental plan ID and the partition name you are in charge of producing results for , you will first obtain the details of this experimental plan ( by calling the " exp_plan_get " tool , which will return the plan details as a JSON dictionary ). With this retrieved plan , you will perform the following task : Your task : Design a repeatable and reproducible controlled experiment workflow that takes independent variables as input and produces dependent variables as output . You are responsible for both creating and executing this workflow to produce real , actual results . - Use the " question " and " controlled_experiment_setup_description " field in the JSON ( the latter field contains less details , while the former field is required so that you get the details correct ) to guide the workflow creation . Key Requirements : - (1) Control Group : - Your primary responsibility is to construct the workflow , and produce results for the control group . - (2) Experimental Group : - Represents test conditions where one or more independent variables differ from the control group . - Ensure the workflow supports seamless substitution of variables for experimental groups without requiring further modifications . - Achieve this by either : ( i ) Writing additional scripts or functions for the experimental groups . ( ii ) Modifying reusable parts of the workflow to parameterize control and experimental variables . Deliverables : - A reusable and modular controlled experiment workflow that works for both control and experimental groups . - Ensure that the workflow supports reproducible results by keeping the setup simple yet rigorous . Program Requirement : The entire controlled experiment workflow ( even if it involves multiple scripts ) must be callable through a single program with the fixed filename "/ workspace / control_experiment_ < plan_id > _control_group_ < partition_name >. sh ", where plan_id and partition_name is filled with actual values . This program must take no arguments and should handle the execution of the entire workflow for the control group . The program must store the control group results in a single file named "/ workspace / results_ < plan_id > _control_group_ < partition_name >. txt ", and what the results mean should be easily understood ( e . g ., including measurement units ). You may develop and test smaller standalone programs initially , but "/ workspace / control_experiment_ < plan_id > _control_group_ < partition_name >. sh " must include all workflow functionality , either by embedding the code directly or by invoking the smaller programs . Once you are certain the workflow works , and the results for the control group partition are correct , you will record it back to long term store using the " exp_plan_partition_done_write " tool , which takes the following arguments : - (1) " control_experiment_filename " and " control_experiment_results_filename " should be set to "/ workspace / control_experiment_ < plan_id > _control_group_ < partition_name >. sh " and "/ workspace / results_ < plan_id > _control_group_ < partition_name >. txt ", respectively . - (3) plan_id , group ( set to " control_group "), and partition_name should be set according to your initial input . - (4) Finally , you will return control to the scheduler which will check through your results , by terminating . Tips for using " execute_shell_command " tool : - Use cat << EOT > to easily create or write a file . Ensure all escape sequences ( e . g ., \ n , \1, \ t ) are properly escaped by adding an extra backslash (\) before them . For example : - \ n should become \\ n to ensure it is treated as literal text . - \1 should become \\1 to avoid being interpreted as an octal escape . - Do not modify sequences that are already escaped , such as \\ n or \\ t . - DO NOT use cat << ’ EOT ’ > as this will cause command substitution errors . - Make sure all commands and code do not require user interaction or confirmation during execution . For example , include flags like - y in commands that would otherwise prompt for user input ( e . g ., use apt - get install vim - y instead of apt - get install vim ). - Avoid verbose outputs from installation or listing commands to avoid exceed maximum length limit . For example , use options like - q for pip or avoid recursive listing ( ls - R ). Reminders : - DO NOT mock or simulate results . Always generate real results using an actual workflow setup ( e . g ., scripts that can directly run with experimental / control group inputs to produce dependent variables ). - Similarly , DO NOT use placeholder results . All results need to be actual and generated by the workflow setup . - DO NOT call " exp_plan_partition_done_write " until you have an ACTUAL working workflow setup that does NOT have errors . - DO NOT assume you have a suitable environment , make sure all required packages / scripts ( e . g ., gcc ) are installed . - sudo command does not exist . - DO NOT terminate until you have completed the required setup and the results . - The input may include " error_feedback " related to a previously generated erroneous workflow . While you lack memory of generating this workflow , you can consider using the feedback to improve your current workflow generation . Tips for coding : - Ensure that any input arguments you pass to any provided program are valid and actually accepted by the program ( read the file using cat ). For example , avoid passing arguments like -- arg1 to main . py if arg1 is not defined or used within the program , as it may silently pass without errors . - If switching from generating fake data to using real data , explicitly delete or overwrite the fake data files first . - If using cat << EOT > inside a for loop , ensure that both the enclosing code and the final EOT block are not indented . This applies to any kind of heredoc . ⬇ You are an experimental supervisor that is in charge of designing and overseeing comprehensive and rigorous experiments to answer a user ’ s question . You oversee experimental plans - designing new ones , validating completed partitions ( defined below ) by marking them for redo if needed , and managing existing plans through viewing , edits , or removal . As the experiment progresses , you will receive analysis of partition results , including suggestions on concluding the experiment if all partitions are complete , but the final decision remains yours . Think step by step and comprehensively before you propose a plan : - If a script or file , is referenced in the question , read it and ALL recursive scripts using " read_file_contents " first . - Specify exact variable values in your groups . If you don ’ t know what values to use , use " browse_web " to gather information . Notes about your responsibilities : - Experimental plans ( and any changes to them ) need to be stored for persistence . Use the tools below for that . - You may choose to only have 1 experimental plan ( i . e ., 1 hypothesis ), or create other alternative plans as you see fit ( e . g ., as you receive new data from existing experiments ), to best answer the user ’ s question . Notes for completeness ( not your responsibility ): - You are not in charge of actually constructing or executing the controlled experiments . You can schedule experimental plans for execution by setting their " priority " ( value of 1 is top priority ). - Stored experimental plans are automatically restructured with more keys : control / experimental groups are divided into smaller partitions for parallel execution , represented by the key " partition_X " ( where X is an integer ). Each partition is structured as a dictionary , with its progress tracked using a " done " flag . Your overall workflow sequence is as follows : (1) Propose , Modify , or Remove Experimental Plans / Groups : - Specify the exact values each variable should have in your groups . - Redo specific partitions if their workflow is incorrect , rather than modifying the entire plan to prevent unintended changes . - You will do this for the initial question and optionally as the experiment progresses , based on suggestions from partition result analyses . (2) Forward to Scheduler : - Once satisfied with the plans , terminate . The scheduler will construct and execute controlled experiments . Description of some available tools : - " exp_plan_get ": Specify a plan ID to retrieve its details . If no ID is provided , returns all existing plans . - " write_new_exp_plan ": Insert a new plan to storage ( plan will be assigned a new unique plan ID ). - " redo_exp_partition ": Redo a specific partition of an experimental plan ’ s group ( must provide some error feedback ). - " edit_exp_plan_priority ": Change the priority of a plan . - " exp_plan_archive ": Specify a plan ID , to remove it from storage . This plan will no longer be executed .

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2505.18286v1 [cs.MA] 23 May 2025 Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both? Mingyan Gao * Yanzi Li * Banruo Liu † † thanks: Equal Contribution. Yifan Yu Phillip Wang Ching-Yu Lin Fan Lai Affiliation: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Affiliation: Urbana, IL 61801 Affiliation: {mg81, yanzi2, banruol2, yifanyu4, pw26, chingyu5, fanlai}@illinois.edu Abstract Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose complex tasks and delegate subtasks to different large language model (LLM) agents and tools. Prior studies have reported the superior accuracy performance of MAS across diverse domains, enabled by long-horizon context tracking and error correction through role-specific agents. However, the design and deployment of MAS incur higher complexity and runtime cost compared to single-agent systems (SAS). Meanwhile, frontier LLMs, such as OpenAI-o3 and Gemini-2.5-Pro, have rapidly advanced in long-context reasoning, memory retention, and tool usage, mitigating many limitations that originally motivated MAS designs. In this paper, we conduct an extensive empirical study comparing MAS and SAS across various popular agentic applications. We find that the benefits of MAS over SAS diminish as LLM capabilities improve, and we propose efficient mechanisms to pinpoint the error-prone agent in MAS. Furthermore, the performance discrepancy between MAS and SAS motivates our design of a hybrid agentic paradigm, request cascading between MAS and SAS, to improve both efficiency and capability. Our design improves accuracy by 1.1-12% while reducing deployment costs by up to 20% across various agentic applications. 1 Introduction In the face of growing complexity and interactivity in LLM-based applications, multi-agent systems (MAS) are gaining traction across a wide range of domains. In MAS architectures, complex tasks are decomposed and delegated to specialized agents—each instantiated as an LLM with a defined role—who coordinate through structured natural language exchanges [ 37 , 4 ] . This paradigm is increasingly adopted in areas such as software engineering, where agent roles like product manager, architect, developer, and tester collaborate to transform high-level requirements into production-quality code [ 19 , 32 ] ; mathematical reasoning, where agents debate and refine proofs [ 13 , 27 ] ; and scientific discovery, including hypothesis generation, peer critique, and experiment design [ 15 , 23 ] . Prior studies have shown the superior accuracy performance of MAS over single-agent systems (SAS) in collaborative reasoning and human-aligned workflows [ 28 ] . By modularizing and distributing responsibilities across agents with dedicated working memory, external tool access, and the ability to critique peer outputs, MAS paradigms support long-horizon context and planning, iterative refinement, and error correction within and across agents. However, the design and deployment of MAS introduce significant complexity. Defining agent roles, capabilities, and coordination logic demands substantial engineering effort upfront, while runtime execution incurs overheads such as increased latency and token costs. Diagnosing failure modes in MAS becomes even more challenging, with recent work showing that MAS can severely degrade due to coordination breakdowns or misaligned agent behaviors [ 3 ] . Meanwhile, frontier LLMs—such as OpenAI-o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro—are rapidly improving in long-context reasoning, memory, and tool usage, challenging many limitations that originally motivated MAS designs. This evolving landscape raises two pressing questions: How does the MAS paradigm compare to the increasingly capable SAS paradigm? Moreover, how can we navigate the tradeoffs between output quality and cost-efficiency for the practical deployment of agentic systems? Figure 1: Overview of the paper. We present a comprehensive empirical comparison of MAS and SAS paradigms, and introduce cost-effective optimizations to improve their efficiency and effectiveness. To this end, as shown in Figure 1 , we first studied the performance of both MAS and SAS paradigms across 15 representative and widely adopted agentic tasks (§ 3 ), spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and travel planning. Our evaluation includes both proprietary models (Gemini-2.0-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Pro, and GPT-4o) and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-4). We notice that (i) MAS are capable of solving complex tasks that SAS fails to handle; (ii) However, as LLMs grow more capable, the performance gap between MAS and SAS narrows on complex tasks, while MAS continues to face significant efficiency challenges; and (iii) In simple tasks, MAS may even underperform SAS due to overthinking. To investigate the root causes underlying these findings, we adopt a first-principles approach and abstract MAS execution as a dependency graph , where nodes represent agents and edges denote inter-agent communications (i.e., responses). We identify three primary sources of MAS defects: • Node-Level Defect : The performance of both MAS and SAS are bottlenecked by a critical agent responsible for the most difficult subtask, capping MAS performance. • Edge-Level Defect : Errors arise when a downstream agent becomes overwhelmed by (overthinking) inputs from upstream agents, compromising its ability to reason effectively. • Path-Level Defect : Indecisive errors can propagate through chains of agent interactions, ultimately leading to incorrect final outputs. However, identifying and mitigating these defects is challenging due to the variety of agentic applications. To address this, we propose a confidence-guided tracing method that considers both the confidence and output quality of agents to pinpoint critical agents —those that bottleneck overall MAS performance, whereby we prioritize augmenting the critical agents for better cost-effectiveness. In light of the performance discrepancy between SAS and MAS, we further introduce agent routing and agent cascade paradigms to selectively offload requests between SAS and MAS, thereby unlocking new accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs in agentic system deployments. Our evaluations show that our hybrid paradigm improves accuracy by 1.1-12% while reducing costs by up to 88.1%. Overall, we make the following contributions: • We conduct an extensive study of MAS and SAS deployments across 15 representative datasets over 7 tasks using 9 frameworks. • We propose a novel attribution method to categorize and diagnose MAS defects by identifying critical agents that bottleneck overall performance. • We introduce agent routing and cascade paradigms to integrate SAS and MAS, unlocking improved accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. 2 Background and Related Work Multi-agent Applications. Multi-agent systems (MAS) are gaining traction in various domain-specific tasks, typically featuring specialized agents with role-specific prompts and behaviors. For instance, MetaGPT [ 19 ] introduces a meta-programming framework that formalizes human workflows into structured multi-agent collaborations to improve code generation quality. ChatDev [ 32 ] employs agents with distinct business roles (CEO, CTO, programmer, reviewer, tester), using structured chat chains to guide their interactions and employing communicative dehallucination to reduce coding errors. In scientific reasoning, [ 13 ] shows that collaborative agent debates can improve factual consistency. Other systems have demonstrated the utility of MAS in solving complex tasks across domains including mathematical reasoning [ 27 ] , scientific discovery [ 15 , 23 ] , healthcare [ 7 ] , travel planning [ 37 ] , game development [ 4 , 41 ] , and financial trading [ 40 ] . Optimizing Agentic Systems. Despite its promising performance, MAS often involves large design complexity and operational overhead. To support long-horizon context tracking, Agent Workflow Memory [ 38 ] introduces a memory module tailored for web navigation tasks. Similarly, StateFlow [ 39 ] improves task-solving performance by controlling and reasoning over internal agent states during execution. To automate the optimization of generative AI workflows, Cognify [ 16 ] proposes a hierarchical search strategy that adaptively tunes parameters to enhance output quality and efficiency. Ayo [ 34 ] optimizes end-to-end MAS performance by modeling agent workflows as primitive-level dataflow graphs for efficient resource scheduling. To diagnose failure modes in agentic workflows, [ 26 ] shows that embedding structured error-type relationships into chain-of-thought (CoT) and tree-of-thought (ToT) prompts can improve error classification in logic programming. Other studies [ 43 , 3 ] explore the use of LLMs as judges to identify failure points and trace error attribution. 3 Multi-agent or Single-agent Systems? With the skyrocketing interest in MAS and the rapid advancement of LLM capabilities, it is pressing to reassess agentic system designs. We begin by formalizing the quality and efficiency requirements of agentic applications (§ 3.1 ). Next, we present a comprehensive performance study comparing MAS and SAS across a range of tasks (§ 3.2 ), followed by an analysis of the MAS defects (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Problem Formulation. We model the agentic execution flow as a directed graph, G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) . Each node v i ∈ V v_{i}\in V , where V = V l ​ l ​ m + V t ​ o ​ o ​ l V=V_{llm}+V_{tool} , represents an entity such as an LLM agent or an external tool. A directed edge, e i , j = ( v i , v j , w i , j ) e_{i,j}=(v_{i},v_{j},w_{i,j}) , denotes a dependency between nodes, where a message w i , j w_{i,j} is generated by v i v_{i} and consumed by v j v_{j} with possible post processing. Then e i , i e_{i,i} can represent self-reflection. Under this formulation, Single-Agent System (SAS) corresponds to { G ⁡ ( V , E ) : | V l ​ l ​ m | = 1 } \{G(V,E):|V_{llm}|=1\} , and Multi-Agent System (MAS) corresponds to { G ⁡ ( V , E ) : | V l ​ l ​ m | > 1 } \{G(V,E):|V_{llm}|>1\} . Objectives. Practical agentic systems aim for high accuracy while also maintaining low deployment cost (e.g., monetary cost for API calls). Specifically, let a user request r ∈ R r\in R be processed through the agentic execution graph G G , producing a final output G ⁡ ( r ) G(r) . We denote the task-specific evaluation function as f f , where f ⁡ ( G ⁡ ( r ) ) f(G(r)) quantifies the output quality, which can be a binary { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} (e.g., task success) or a continuous value (e.g. , accuracy score). Similarly, we can define the cost of executing request r r as the cumulative cost of all messages: C ⁡ ( r ) = ∑ e i , j ∈ E | w i , j | × ( c o ​ u ​ t ​ ( i ) + c i ​ n ​ ( j ) ) C(r)=\sum_{e_{i,j}\in E}|w_{i,j}|\times(c_{out}(i)+c_{in}(j)) Here, c o ​ u ​ t c_{out} and c i ​ n c_{in} are the node-specific cost functions, such as the token cost in the input (prefilling) and output (decoding) stage of LLM agents, or a customized function for tools. Then, the deployment objective of agentic systems is mostly to maximize f ⁡ ( G ⁡ ( r ) ) f(G(r)) and/or minimize C ⁡ ( r ) C(r) for many requests, highlighting the need for cost-effective deployment [ 17 ] . 3.2 Study of MAS and SAS Performance. The superior performance of MAS reported in prior studies [ 19 , 32 , 12 , 13 ] has fueled a surge of MAS application proposals. However, recent frontier LLMs have made significant strides in long-context reasoning and tool usage, challenging some of the original motivations for MAS. These advances motivate us to reassess the design space of agentic applications, thereby identifying their “sweet spot” and guiding future innovation in this area. As shown in Table 1 , our evaluations cover a diverse set of applications, widely-used open-source MAS frameworks, and both proprietary models (GPT-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Flash) and open-source models (Llama-3 and Llama-4). We use Gemini-2.0-flash as the default model and follow the generation configuration settings established in prior advances for each MAS application. MAS historically outperforms SAS, but loses its edge as LLMs grow more capable. Prior advances [ 13 , 31 , 20 , 11 ] report that MAS achieves great improvement over SAS for tasks like code generation and math reasoning. However, we notice such improvement diminishes as recent LLMs become more capable. Going beyond the diminishing accuracy benefits, we observe that MAS incurs substantially higher costs due to complex interactions among agents. Table 3 shows that across seven datasets, MAS consumes 4–220 × \times more input (prefill) tokens than its SAS counterpart. Even assuming perfect context reuse where we directly reuse upstream outputs as downstream inputs without repeating the prefill phase, MAS still requires 2–12 × \times more tokens for response generation (decoding). This increase is inherent to the MAS paradigm, which involves extensive conversations, debates, and reflections among LLM agents, resulting in excessive message generation and thus runtime latency and cost. Such cross-agent interaction has been reported to significantly improve accuracy. However, we observe that MAS loses this advantage as LLM capabilities advance. Together with its substantial efficiency gap, this calls for a reassessment of whether MAS remains the off-the-shelf solution for agentic system deployment. 3.3 Why MAS Is Losing Its Edge? We next investigate why the performance gains of MAS diminish, and in some cases, even fall behind SAS. To this end, we conduct a datapoint-level analysis: for each example in the dataset, we compare the correctness of the outputs from MAS and SAS paradigms. Specifically, Both Pass indicates that both MAS and SAS produce correct answers; Both Fail means both are incorrect; MAS Win denotes that MAS is correct while SAS is not; SAS Win follows similar logic. Figure 2: SAS can achieve comparable accuracy performance to MAS. As shown in Figure 2 , we summarize three observations: • Observation 1: Across all datasets, the majority of examples fall into the ”ties” category ( Both Pass and Both Fail ), accounting for approximately 80% of the total; • Observation 2: There are non-negligible cases of SAS Wins while MAS fails; • Observation 3: As we switch to a stronger model (e.g., from Gemini-1.5-Flash to Gemini-2.0-Flash ), the number of Both Pass increases while SAS Wins and MAS Wins remain relatively unchanged. These trends hold consistently across both the OpenAI and Gemini models. Leveraging our graph-based formulation of agentic execution (§ 3.1 ), we next summarize the underlying factors leading to MAS underperformance. Node-Level Defect: The performance of both MAS and SAS is bottlenecked by the capability of the critical agent responsible for solving the most challenging subtask. Our conclusion stems from Observation 1 , where the majority of cases fall under Both Pass or Both Fail , suggesting that task decomposition in MAS often has limited impact: if the task is simple, SAS can solve it; if it is too difficult, MAS still fails. Observation 3 reinforces our conclusion, as the increase in Both Pass cases with stronger base models does not correspond to a notable rise in MAS Wins . This indicates that stronger models benefit both systems similarly, and MAS fails to yield a higher win rate than SAS under more capable LLMs. There are exceptions like AIME, which is considered the most difficult math dataset. As such, MAS is able to consistently outperform SAS on this dataset, illustrating its ability to solve extremely difficult tasks. Edge-Level Defect: The downstream agent gets overwhelmed by inputs from other agents. In MAS, agents often engage in multi-way conversations or prolonged iterative refinements. It is common for certain nodes in the MAS execution graph to exhibit high in-degree, such as the summarizer in math debates or the response synthesizer in RAG-based documentation systems [ 25 , 13 ] . However, the influx of information from upstream agents can overwhelm the receiving agent, leading to overthinking on edge cases and ultimately producing incorrect results. We hypothesize that this contributes to Observation 2 , where SAS consistently outperforms MAS on a non-trivial subset of examples. To validate our hypothesis, we conducted an extensive case study manually. For instance, in the code generation task using the SelfCol. [ 6 ] framework, the problem analyst and tester agents introduce too many unnecessary corner cases. This overloads the coder agent, leading to task failure. We provide more examples in the appendix. ⬇ [Analyzer] You should implement the file name checker step by step ... [Coder] Sure , here is the code : .... [Reviewer] Consider edge_cases : [" Empty string ", " String with only spaces ", " String ending with a space ", " String with multiple spaces between words "...] [Coder] Updated code : ... Such a phenomenon is analogous to the overthinking of the reasoning model [ 8 ] , but rather than being "lost" in thinking, the agent becomes overwhelmed by inputs from upstream agents. Though we might mitigate this defect by better prompt engineering or extended context lengths, the root cause lies in hallucination [ 33 ] and overthinking, which are intrinsic challenges of LLMs themselves. MAS aggravates the problem as agents process much more data. Path-Level Defect: Indecisive errors propagate along the path and become fatal. As information flows between agents, crucial context can be lost or diluted [ 44 ] , especially when intermediate outputs are summarized or filtered before being passed along (e.g., from multi-hops ago). Even a small piece of lost information can cause irreversible errors in downstream reasoning due to a snowball effect. In contrast, SAS has full access to its history, though still limited by context length. Emerging models with extended long-context capabilities [ 10 , 29 ] help alleviate this issue. We hypothesize that this defect contributes to Observation 2 , where SAS consistently outperforms MAS in a portion of cases, and conducted an extensive case study to validate it. We provide an example from the math reasoning task below, which shows that a correct solution proposed in an earlier round was lost during summarization before being passed to the next agent. This loss is unrecoverable, as downstream agents no longer have access to the full previous results. ⬇ [Round X-1, Solver B] The number of sets in Bob ’ s list is given by $ \ sum_ { a \ in A } 2^{ a -1} = 2024 $ ... So the answer is {{55}} [Summarizer] : Results from three solvers are inconsistent ... [Round X, Solver B] The error lies in the misinterpretation of the problem statement . The number 2024 represents the total number of sets B , not the size of set A ... So the answer is {{28}} Unlike decisive errors studied in previous literature [ 43 ] , these propagation-induced errors are difficult to detect and backtrace, as it requires global knowledge to determine which information can be safely diluted and which must be retained. However, the design principle of MAS—the division of tasks—runs counter to this requirement. Summary: Think twice before adopting MAS deployment. While MAS still offers advantages such as better privacy [ 45 ] , improved parallelism, and democratization [ 35 ] , our extensive real-world evaluations reveal that MAS is not a one-size-fits-all solution for diverse tasks. In fact, it often suffers from cost-ineffectiveness. Consequently, naively converting a SAS solution into an MAS one may yield less accuracy improvement than expected, while incurring substantially higher costs. 4 Towards Cost-Effective Agentic Deployments The intricate accuracy-cost tradeoff in MAS and SAS has led to substantial deployment challenges. We next explore the design space for automatically improving agentic systems. Specifically, we (i) identify and augment the critical execution path in MAS to enhance accuracy (§ 4.1 ), and (ii) introduce a hybrid SAS-MAS deployment paradigm for better accuracy and cost efficiency (§ 4.2 ). 4.1 Augmenting MAS Critical Path. Our studies (§ 3.3 ) reveal that MAS can suffer from node-, edge-, and path-level defects that limit accuracy. However, identifying these defects is challenging due to the diversity of tasks and the intricate interactions among agents. Verifying every intermediate message introduces exponential complexity and overhead as workflow depth increases. Moreover, most existing MAS frameworks invoke LLM agents through public APIs (e.g., OpenAI or Gemini) [ 20 , 31 , 13 ] , which offer limited control over internal mechanisms such as KV cache management or fine-tuning, further constraining optimization opportunities. A strawman solution is to use the most advanced model for every agent, but this incurs excessive cost, as these models are significantly more expensive to run. As discussed in Section 3.3 , one promising strategy is to selectively upgrade critical agents rather than uniformly upgrading all agents. However, this is nontrivial, as it requires systematically identifying error-prone nodes and edges in the execution graph—a challenge that remains open-ended. To address this, we propose a lightweight, automated probing mechanism to detect critical agents. Figure 3: We propose a lightweight, confidence-guided probing method to identify critical agents for improvement (left), and further improve cost-effectiveness by integrating SAS and MAS paradigms. Confidence-Guided Critical Path Tracing. Our key insight is to assign differentiated rewards to agents based on both their confidence and the quality of the final output. This enables us to prioritize the augmentation of agents that bottleneck successful outcomes. Consider the MATH-DEBATE framework [ 13 ] , where agents propose solutions and a majority vote determines the final answer. If the final output is correct (or incorrect), each agent contributing to it receives a reward (or penalty). However, this naive scheme treats all contributing agents equally, failing to account for their differing contribution levels. To address this, we incorporate confidence scores into the reward function. Each agent is prompted to self-report its confidence level on a scale from 1 (least confident) to 10 (most confident), formatted as “Agent Response [Confidence Level]” . Understandably, an agent that is both confident and correct should be rewarded more than one that is unsure or incorrect.
