Augmenting the critical path makes MAS more suitable for complex problems that benefit from specialized roles. However, this still comes at deployment cost. In contrast, SAS tends to be more efficient and effective for simpler, well-scoped tasks. More subtly, investing more resources in MAS does not necessarily yield better performance than SAS (§ 3.2 ). As such, one would expect a hybrid paradigm that strategically combines MAS and SAS to leverage their respective design sweet spots. However, integrating MAS and SAS paradigms is non-trivial due to the wide variability in task complexity and application domains. Moreover, a practical solution must be request-dependent and cost-efficient. To this end, we introduce two primary strategies: Agent Routing and Agent Cascade for different scenarios. Agent Routing. The key idea behind agent routing is to use an LLM-based rater to assess the complexity of each request and decide whether to route it to an SAS or MAS system. This strategy is broadly applicable across diverse workloads. Here, the rater assigns a difficulty score to each incoming request. Based on a user-defined threshold, requests with scores above the threshold are routed to MAS, while those below are handled by SAS. The routing design offers users flexibility to balance accuracy and cost. Suppose a proportion p p of requests are routed to MAS, and the remaining ( 1 − p 1-p ) to SAS. Then, the total cost of agent routing can be defined as: C Rater ​ ( r ) + p ⋅ C MAS ​ ( r ) + ( 1 − p ) ⋅ C SAS ​ ( r ) , C_{\text{Rater}}(r)+p\cdot C_{\text{MAS}}(r)+(1-p)\cdot C_{\text{SAS}}(r), where C ⁡ ( r ) C(r) denotes the cost of processing request r r . The rater adds only minimal overhead because it relies on a system prompt that can be effectively cached and produces only a small, constant number of tokens representing the difficulty score. The accuracy of this routing approach depends on the rater’s capability and the choice of the threshold value. Nonetheless, we observe that agent routing generally achieves higher accuracy than SAS and, with a properly selected threshold value (routing easy requests to SAS and hard requests to MAS), it can even outperform MAS (§ 3.3 ). We attribute MAS underperformance to node-, edge-, and path-level defects, and introduce a confidence-guided tracing method to identify critical agents. To optimize cost-effectiveness, we propose a hybrid agentic paradigm that selectively offloads requests between MAS and SAS, achieving up to 12% better accuracy and 88.1% cost savings. Our findings offer actionable insights for deploying adaptive, cost-efficient agentic systems. Limitation : Although in this paper, we did extensive analysis across tasks, frameworks, and models, our experiments are mostly focused on agentic systems built upon general-purpose models, rather than fine-tuned models. In addition, this paper focuses on agentic systems for task solving, despite they are the most popular ones. We left those unexplored areas as future work. Broader Impact : This paper challenges the prevailing assumption that MAS outperforms SAS in terms of accuracy. We identify that this misconception arises from fundamental limitations inherent to agentic frameworks. We further advocate for future research in multi-agent systems to place greater emphasis on deployment efficiency rather than accuracy alone. B.2 Confidence Based Tracing We request the agent to output the confidence by concatenating the following prompt to the original prompt: ⬇ Also , provide your confidence in your answer on a scale from 1 ( least confident ) to 10 ( most confident ), in the form : Confidence : X . We will extract the confidence score using regular expressions. The confidence score is recorded for each round. When neither agent reaches an agreement during the majority voting, we will choose the agent with the highest confidence score. We next study whether the system’s performance grows as we increase the number of agents in it. We use the Debate framework in the Math Reasoning task, and change the number of solves during the debate. Figure 8 shows that most of the time, when we increase the number of solves, the accuracy does not increase. Actually, we notice that even if we only use one agent, the result is still comparable to using more agents. This finding only confirms our Node Defect hypothesis that the whole performance is bounded by the critical agents—weak agents cannot solve the math problem are essentially guessing, and it does not help when we just increase the number of random guesses. We also conduct the experiment of the effect of Summarize (i.e., pass the summary of the previous round to the next round) or just Concatenate (i.e., just dump everything from the previous round to the next round). From Figure 8 , we observe that there is not much difference for the Gemini-2.0-Flash model, while Summarize is worse than Concatenate when using weak models. This also confirms our hypothesis on Path Defect , where the weak summarizer will inevitably lose critical information from the previous round, leading to an accuracy drop. Impact of Number of Reflection Rounds. We further investigate whether self-reflection helps improve MAS performance. We use the Debate framework for the Math Reasoning task. Figure 9 shows that increasing the number of rounds of debate (reflection) increases accuracy in AIME, but decreases accuracy in GSM8K. This further confirms our Edge Defect hypothesis, where too much redundant information on easy tasks actually makes agents confused and obsessed with corner cases, thus losing accuracy, while reflection on complicated problems is effective.
